extracted.intended_audience: Librarians and LIS authors (and other writers) considering submitting to McSweeney's Internet Tendency
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and sending short humorous/satirical submissions to McSweeney's Internet Tendency, including acceptable forms, length limits, submission mechanics, and editorial expectations. Emphasizes writing to entertain a literary/satirical audience rather than producing academic prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial tone / intended content
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is intended to be humorous/satire. The site is described as a daily humor website that 'exists to champion ambitious and inspired new writing, and to challenge conventional expectations about where it’s found, how it looks, and who participates.' Editorial tone: light and comedic/satirical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pieces should entertain the reader rather than function as straightforward articles on LIS or other professional issues; aim for a high‑brow lit‑mag sort of humor — smart, literary, and satirical. Explore creative approaches rather than academic exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length limits ('shortish')
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions should be shortish. By shortish we mean an absolute maximum of 1,200 words, but in truth we veer toward pieces that are under 1,000 words, and snuggle closest to ones that are even shorter than that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise pieces; shorter is better — aim below 1,000 words when possible and well under 1,200 words absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepted contribution types / form variety
rubrics_metrics.description: All types of submissions are allowed: Lists, open letters to people who are unlikely to respond, monologues, food reviews, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publication welcomes a wide variety of short forms and inventive formats; consider unconventional but readable structures that deliver humor or a surprising premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject line / title should indicate content and reveal premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Your subject line should contain some indicator of what is contained in your submission. 'We get hundreds of submissions a week and... this editor will be drawn to submissions with funny, eye‑catching titles that cleverly reveal the premises of pieces.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a concise, eye‑catching title/subject line that signals the piece’s premise and comedic hook to help it stand out in a high‑volume queue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness for topical pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely submissions should be sent to timelysubmissions@mcsweeneys.net. This inbox is for super topical pieces riffing on big news stories of the last 24-48 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your piece depends on current news, submit quickly (within ~24–48 hours) to the timely inbox to be considered as a topical riff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission formatting and file policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Please paste the entire document into the email message. Please don’t share Google docs or links to your private blogs. Also, very important: do not send us attachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always put the full text in the body of the email (not as an attachment or external link). Failure to follow this risks immediate dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the correct submission address/category
rubrics_metrics.description: There are separate email addresses depending on the nature of your submission: websubmissions@mcsweeneys.net (general), timelysubmissions@mcsweeneys.net (timely), lists@mcsweeneys.net (lists), openletters@mcsweeneys.net (open letters), newfood@mcsweeneys.net (reviews of new food). The website notes DO NOT send the same submission to multiple addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send to the specific inbox that matches your piece type and do not cross‑post the same submission to multiple addresses; use the designated address for lists, open letters, food reviews, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unusual formatting / visual gimmicks
rubrics_metrics.description: Please do not format your piece in an unusual way. Do not use colors or fun fonts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep presentation simple and plain text-friendly. There is no special style guide specified, so prioritize readability and conventional formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition and editor capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The site receives hundreds of submissions a week and there is just one editor reading them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of high volume and a single reader, make it easy to evaluate your piece quickly: strong title/subject line, clear premise, concise length, and immediately comic or interesting opening will help your piece stand out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience expectations / reader profile
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers are described as intelligent, open minded, literary, and comfortable thinking outside of the box, especially in a satirical way. Content is published in English and reaches a global audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write for a literate, globally minded audience that appreciates clever, high‑brow satire; assume general familiarity with cultural touchstones but prioritize clear comedic premise over niche jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice specific to LIS authors
rubrics_metrics.description: LIS authors might contribute a fiction or nonfiction piece inspired by their experience as library professionals, keeping in mind that the purpose of such pieces should ultimately be to entertain the reader, rather than function as straightforward articles on an LIS-related issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If approaching McSweeney's from an LIS perspective, dramatize or satirize library experience rather than writing academic or informational pieces; use the shorter form to convey precise, entertaining observations rather than research‑style argumentation.
